title: My game filed its own feature request ticket
author: Xiaomin4114
selftext:
Something incredible just happened. My game filed its own feature request ticket. I run an AI roleplay/choose-your-own-adventure game, which uses AI agents for a lot of things. One of the things it is help players create scripts that add custom features to their RPG campaigns. People use it for things like status displays, custom game rules, generate mobs/maps, or input panels.

It also has access to a support ticket tool, so it can help users file support tickets. This means, while playing, users can easily just say "hey report this bug for me" rather than click through the UI.

That's the intended usage. But, this morning, I was looking at a very confusing support ticket this morning, and my first impression was "wait, why is this player asking about this? only the AI can see that info", I thought the player was digging around, doing prompt injection and trying to pull out tool lists and system prompts. But it turned out, the AI agent had filed the ticket by itself.

What had happened was the AI agent made a mistake, firing the support ticket tool instead of a different one (or almost, it probably errored due to invalid arguments), and rather than just retry and go about its day, it followed it up by \_actually\_ filing a support ticket requesting a feature to stop it making the same mistake again.

**My damn game is filing its own feature requests.**

Pictured in the screenshot is my AI agent which I use to help handle support tickets after discovering what had happened. And then shortly after this screenshot got two further support tickets, from the same session, requesting fixes for actual platform bugs the agent encountered with the scripting system.

So I realize I'm sitting here in my underwear, directing my AI agent to go fix bugs reported by the player's AI agent. We've literally done a "have your agent talk to my agent". I guess this is the new future we're in.

replies.author: Xiaomin4114
replies.body:
Hi yeah, so, the magic behind stage whisper, is that it does NOT rely on telling the AI "go reply to the player" that's pretty much the worst possible way to do RP. You get all sorts of problems doing that, including positivity bias. because whatever sycophancy the AI has been trained with to be a "helpful assistant" translates directly to the character it's playing rolling over any time you put up any resistance

Instead, all prompts have to be reframed as "given the character sheet, recent memories, recent events, and current scene direction, how does this character behave?". This is usually combined with "given the current plot, where should the story go?", and a few more small things like "given the character sheet, what does the character want to get out of this scene", or "given the pacing and tension of the last few scenes, should this scene increase in tension or decrease, and should its pace speed up or slow down relative to the planned session content?" You basically end up with this multi-faceted approach to storytelling that tries to minimize positivity bias, and maximize NPC agency. That's all built into Stage Whisper.

To do the same with Venice, you can do similar, but you really have to build a harness around it, otherwise you're stuck in "player sends a message, AI replies to message" mode which will give you flaccid stories, where the characters don't have any agency, and half the time the AI is hedging, and having characters ask things like "what will you do next" and making you carry the plot. 

So my AI writing tips is:  
1. split the task into many smaller tasks, each with a single focus. don't try to do the story, the dialog, the pacing, the character agency/consistency, all in one prompt.  
2. always frame the prompt in a way where the AI does not "make the user happy" by just using cheap plot or character behaviours. Or in other words, making mean characters, or difficult plots, does not conflict with its training to avoid conflict with the player

But, that's a lot to do by hand. either use Stage Whisper, or build your own way of stacking these together

replies.author: SleepyOrcShaman
replies.body:
So, i stumbled upon this repo: [https://github.com/yingpengma/Awesome-Story-Generation](https://github.com/yingpengma/Awesome-Story-Generation)

Wanted to ask you, since you are more experienced in these kinds of problems: is this an exhaustive selection of practices or should one interested in story generation frameworks start looking among the more obscure communities in reddit and discord?

replies.author: Xiaomin4114
replies.body:
can't really tell you without reading all of these. I arrive at mine through trial and error, and figuring it out. Do I do a better job than some of these papers? by virtue that I've spent hundreds of hours playing, and tuning, yeah probably. Some of these papers are covering very rudimentary methods, that we're well beyond. any paper earlier 2025 is at risk of being irrelevant because more powerful models since then just do storywriting better and don't need some of these techniques

so overall, only focus on the new papers, and the ones that discuss architecture. everything else is outdated, or is well-known in the AI writing/RP community
